persona.who: 66, retired bank officer in Lucknow, wife passed 2 years ago, son in Toronto, daughter in Mumbai. Reads the Gita occasionally, wants to understand it properly.
persona.note: after my wife left us the house is very quiet. children call on sunday. I have time now and I want to read Gita properly not just the shlokas everyone forwards on whatsapp

understanding.bridge: The quiet house is what the Upanishads call the self without a name. The Gita you want to read is not a collection of verses but a conversation with what does not pass.
understanding.week_thesis: From the quiet of a house to the quiet of a text, so that the Gita becomes a conversation and not a collection of verses.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From 'Weighing the Lasting and the Passing': a portrait of old age.
verse.sanskrit: गात्रं संकुचितं गतिर्विगलिता भ्रष्टा च दन्तावलिः- दृष्टिर्नश्यति वर्धते बधिरता वक्त्रं च लालायते । वाक्यं नाद्रियते च बान्धवजनो भार्या न शुश्रूषते हा कष्टं पुरुषस्य जीर्णवयसः पुत्रोऽप्यमित्रायते ॥
verse.line: In old age, family stops listening and even a son turns cold. Alas for the aged.
verse.translation: The body shrinks, the gait falters, the teeth fall out, sight fades, deafness grows, the mouth drools; relatives pay no heed to his words, his wife no longer looks after him; alas, the misery of an old man: even his son turns hostile.
verse.why: Do what matters most while you still can.
verse.misuse: A lament, not a prediction; read it as a call to keep listening to the old.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: Weighing the lasting and the passing
prasang.summary: Weighing what lasts: religion without inner peace is trading; old age can bring neglect; act while healthy, not when the house is on fire. The poet admits not knowing how to spend a short life.
prasang.lesson: Do what matters most while you still can.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari sits with the reader and speaks of the body’s slow retreat, the teeth falling, the eyes dimming, the gait faltering. He names the loneliness of being no longer heard, even by a son. He does not say this must be feared. He says this is the moment to listen differently, to act on what matters while the voice still holds. The quiet house is not a warning. It is the ground you stand on now.
verse.for_you: The quiet house is the ground you stand on. It is not a problem to be filled, but the place where what matters most can finally be heard.

verse.speaker: Prajapati's teaching (narrator)
verse.setting: On the self in the heart that we visit nightly in deep sleep without knowing it.
verse.sanskrit: अनृतापिधानास्तद्यथापि हिरण्यनिधिं निहितमक्षेत्रज्ञा उपर्युपरि सञ्चरन्तो न विन्देयुरेवमेवेमाः सर्वाः प्रजा अहरहर्गच्छन्त्य एतं ब्रह्मलोकं न विन्दन्त्यनृतेन हि प्रत्यूढाः ॥
verse.line: Like people walking daily over buried gold, we pass our own treasure every day and never find it.
verse.translation: As people who do not know the spot walk again and again over a hidden treasure of gold buried in the ground and do not find it, so all these creatures go day after day into that world of Brahman and do not find it, for they are carried away by untruth.

matched.label: Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful

verse.meaning: A teacher once said that all beings travel every day into the world of Brahman, yet they never find it. They are like people who do not know the spot, walking again and again over a hidden treasure of gold buried in the ground, and never finding it. They are carried away by untruth. The teaching is that we pass our own treasure every day and never find it. The world we enter in deep sleep is the self in the heart, and we walk right over it.
verse.for_you: You have the Gita in your hands and the quiet of the house around you. The treasure you are looking for is not in the forwarded messages but in the reading itself, closer than the breath, right where you sit.

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
verse.sanskrit: स्वाराज्ये भैक्षवृत्तौ च लाभालाभे जने वने । निर्विकल्पस्वभावस्य न विशेषोऽस्ति योगिनः ॥
verse.line: Throne or begging bowl, gain or loss, crowd or solitude: a steady person stays the same.
verse.translation: For the yogi of steady nature there is no difference between ruling a kingdom and living on alms, gain and loss, the crowd and the forest.
verse.why: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

prasang.title: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

verse.meaning: In a long teaching on peace, a sage once told a king that for the yogi of steady nature, there is no difference between ruling a kingdom and living on alms, gain and loss, the crowd and the forest. Calm is not found by chasing it or changing places. It is how you hold ordinary life.
verse.for_you: The quiet of the house is not a problem to fix. It is the ground you stand on. You do not need to move to a temple or a forest to find what you are looking for. You need only to hold this reading as your own, steady and sure.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse.sanskrit: यदेतत्स्वच्छन्दं विहरणमकार्पण्यमशनं सहार्यैः संवासः श्रुतमुपशमैकव्रतफलम् । मनो मन्दस्पन्दं बहिरपि चिरस्यापि विमृशन् न जाने कस्यैष परिणतिरुदारस्य तपसः ॥
verse.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.
verse.why: Gratitude for a simple life, and devotion without rivalry between forms of God.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: Worship of Shiva
prasang.summary: Devotional verses longing for a quiet life by the Ganga in Shiva's presence, including a famous non-sectarian line that Shiva and Vishnu are one in essence.
prasang.lesson: Gratitude for a simple life, and devotion without rivalry between forms of God.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari sits by the Ganga, looking at a simple life. They say, I do not know what past discipline earned me this freedom to wander, this plain food, this company of good people, and this learning that brings only calm. The mind looks out at the world but stirs gently inside, and they ask what kind of quiet austerity this is the fruit of.
verse.for_you: Sit with the text as you sit with your quiet house, not to fix it, but to let it be. Let the words be a presence, closer than the breath, that does not pass.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna begins his ladder of practices with the simplest instruction.
verse.sanskrit: मय्येव मन आधत्स्व मयि बुद्धिं निवेशय । निवसिष्यसि मय्येव अत ऊर्ध्वं न संशयः ॥
verse.line: Rest your mind in me, settle your thinking in me, and you will live in me.
verse.translation: Fix your mind on me alone, let your understanding settle in me; from then on you will dwell in me. Of this there is no doubt.

matched.label: I want to reconnect with my roots

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna on the battlefield, about to leave for battle. He offers a simple ladder of practices, and he begins with the very first step. The instruction is to fix your mind on me alone. Let your understanding settle in me. Once that happens, you will live in me. This is not about doing more. It is about resting your mind and letting your thinking settle. Then you will dwell in me. There is no doubt about this.
verse.for_you: The house is quiet today. You have time. Try reading one chapter slowly. Do not collect verses. Let the conversation settle, just as Krishna asks Arjuna to let his understanding settle.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna opens the teaching on knowing him fully.
verse.sanskrit: श्री भगवानुवाचमय्यासक्तमनाः पार्थ योगं युञ्जन्मदाश्रयः । असंशयं समग्रं मां यथा ज्ञास्यसि तच्छृणु ॥
verse.line: Keep your mind attached to me, lean on me, keep practising. You will come to know me fully.
verse.translation: Hear, Partha, how with your mind attached to me, practising yoga and taking refuge in me, you will know me fully, without doubt.

matched.label: I want to reconnect with my roots

verse.meaning: Krishna tells Arjuna to fix his mind on him, to take shelter in him, and to keep practicing. This means the way to truly know him is not through doubt or scattered effort. It is through steady, devoted practice. You let your thinking rest in one place and do not waver. The knowing grows from that quiet attention, not from rushing to finish a chapter.
verse.for_you: You have the time now for this. Read one chapter of the Gita slowly, not to collect a verse, but to let the conversation settle. Let the quiet of the house and the quiet of the text meet there.

story.title: Shabari's long wait
story.story_hook: Her teachers had all gone, and still she gathered fruit every day for a guest who had never come.
story.summary: The old ascetic woman Shabari has lived for years at Pampa after her teachers died, told that Ram would one day come. She has kept gathering forest food for him. When he arrives, she welcomes him, shows him her teachers' forest, and departs in peace.
story.lesson: Faithful waiting, unseen by the world, is not wasted.

anchor.speaker: Shabari
anchor.setting: The old ascetic woman Shabari has waited years at Pampa for Ram, as her teachers foretold.
anchor.sanskrit: एवमुक्ता महाभागैस्तदाहं पुरुषर्षभ। मया तु संचितं वन्यं विविधं पुरुषर्षभ॥ तवार्थे पुरुषव्याघ्र पम्पायास्तीरसम्भवम्।
anchor.line: I was told you would come, so I kept gathering for you. Waiting was a kind of preparing.
anchor.translation: So the great ones told me, best of men, and for you I have gathered every kind of forest food from the banks of the Pampa.
anchor.why: Faithful waiting, unseen by the world, is not wasted.

story.hook_title: Shabari, an old woman in the forest, gathered fruit every day for a guest who never came
story.teaser: Shabari, an old woman in the forest, gathered fruit every day for a guest who never came
story.for_you: Shabari waited in a quiet place for a teacher she had never seen, and her waiting was not wasted. You have also gathered what you could for a long time, and now you are here. Your quiet house is not empty. It is the place where the search begins and the conversation finds you.

script: The house is very quiet now, and the weekend calls are a rhythm you have learned to carry. You are searching for something deeper than the verses that reach your phone, a truth that does not pass away.

Bhartrihari sits with the reader and speaks of the body’s slow retreat, the teeth falling, the eyes dimming, the gait faltering. He names the loneliness of being no longer heard, even by a son. He does not say this must be feared. He says this is the moment to listen differently, to act on what matters while the voice still holds. And Bhartrihari says:
गात्रं संकुचितं गतिर्विगलिता भ्रष्टा च दन्तावलिः- दृष्टिर्नश्यति वर्धते बधिरता वक्त्रं च लालायते, वाक्यं नाद्रियते च बान्धवजनो भार्या न शुश्रूषते हा कष्टं पुरुषस्य जीर्णवयसः पुत्रोऽप्यमित्रायते.
In plain words: In old age, family stops listening and even a son turns cold. Alas for the aged.

This is not a lament about the years to come. It is a call to keep listening while there is still breath to speak. The body will retreat and the family will drift, this is true. But the voice that holds the question does not have to fade before you find the answer you are looking for.
Use this time to listen to the Gita as a conversation, not a collection of forwarded messages. Let the text meet you in the quiet, without needing to solve it all at once.
What is the one question you want the text to answer for you?

depth.life: The house is quiet because the world you once moved through is moving on. Your children call, but the silence between their voices is where you live now. You have the time, the Gita, and a sense that the forwarded messages do not reach the real question.
depth.points: What lasts is not the family that grows distant or the body that fades. What lasts is the inner work you can still do while the house is quiet and the mind is still your own. The Gita is not a collection of verses to be forwarded, but a conversation with what remains when everything else has passed.
depth.practice: Open your Gita and read one verse without looking for a forwarded meaning, only the words on the page.
depth.question: What is the first thing you would say to the quiet if it could answer?
